beats.headline: Why does your microservice keep losing events?
beats.subline: The dual-write problem is a silent killer in distributed systems.
beats.narration: You save to PostgreSQL and send to Kafka. If the database rolls back after Kafka sends, or the pod crashes before sending, your system state is permanently corrupted. You cannot fix this with code alone.

beats.title: The Dual-Write Anti-Pattern

top.label: Naive Approach
points: Kafka is not in the DB transaction

bottom.label: Transactional Outbox

beats.narration: The naive approach splits your logic across two systems that don't share a transaction. The Outbox pattern forces the event into the same database transaction as your business state, ensuring atomicity.

beats.title: The Outbox Schema

steps.explanation: Store the event payload and aggregate ID inside your own DB.
Keep polling fast by only indexing pending rows.

beats.narration: Your outbox table acts as a persistent buffer. By using a partial index on pending status, your relay can fetch events without scanning the entire history of your application.

beats.title: Outbox Lifecycle
beats.narration: The service commits both records atomically. A background relay then picks up the event, publishes it to Kafka, and marks it as processed. This is the foundation of reliable event-driven architecture.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.narration: That is the core pattern. In Part 2, we compare the simple polling relay against the high-performance Debezium CDC approach for streaming your outbox events.

beats.headline: Should you poll or stream your outbox?
beats.subline: Choosing the wrong relay strategy will bottleneck your database.
beats.narration: Polling is easy to build, but CDC is the gold standard for scale. Let's look at the trade-offs between simple SQL polling and log-based streaming.

beats.title: Polling with SKIP LOCKED
beats.code:
jdbcClient.sql("""
  SELECT * FROM outbox_events
  WHERE status = 'PENDING'
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 50""")
  .query(OutboxRow.class).list();

steps.explanation: Allows multiple pods to poll the same table without blocking each other.

beats.narration: Use SKIP LOCKED to let multiple instances process the outbox concurrently. It prevents row contention, but beware: it adds load to your database and can cause ordering issues if not sharded correctly.

beats.title: Debezium CDC Pipeline
beats.narration: CDC tails the database WAL log directly. It captures changes without any extra SQL queries, providing sub-millisecond latency and zero polling overhead on your production tables.

beats.title: Polling vs. CDC
beats.narration: Polling is perfect for low-traffic services where simplicity wins. Use Debezium CDC when you need massive throughput and want to avoid the performance tax of constant table scanning.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Polling is simple, CDC is scalable
beats.narration: Now you have the producer side covered. In Part 3, we tackle the consumer side with the Transactional Inbox pattern to handle at-least-once delivery duplicates.

beats.headline: Your consumer will receive the same event twice.
beats.subline: At-least-once delivery is a feature, not a bug.
beats.narration: Kafka guarantees delivery, but network retries mean you will eventually process the same event multiple times. If your logic isn't idempotent, you're going to have a very bad day.

beats.title: The Inbox Pattern

steps.explanation: Use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING to safely ignore repeated events.

beats.narration: The inbox table tracks processed message IDs. By using ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, we ensure the business logic runs exactly once per message, even if Kafka redelivers the record.

beats.title: Inbox Atomicity
beats.narration: The inbox insert and your business logic share the same transaction. If the transaction commits, the event is marked as processed. If it fails, the event remains unprocessed for a retry.

beats.title: The Acknowledge Trap
beats.caption: Where to commit the Kafka offset
beats.narration: Never acknowledge the Kafka offset inside your transaction. If the database commit fails after the offset is acknowledged, the message is lost forever. Always acknowledge after the transaction succeeds.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Ack Kafka offsets after DB commit
beats.narration: You are now building bulletproof event-driven systems. In Part 4, we wrap up with table retention strategies to keep your database lean and performant.

beats.headline: Your outbox table will grow forever.
beats.subline: Unmanaged outbox tables kill database performance.
beats.narration: If you don't clean up your outbox and inbox tables, you'll eventually hit storage limits and index bloat. Here is how to manage retention without locking your production tables.

beats.title: Daily Partitioning

steps.explanation: Partition by date to make cleanup a simple metadata operation.
Dropping a partition is instantaneous compared to DELETE.

beats.narration: Partitioning is the secret to massive scale. Instead of running expensive DELETE queries that bloat your table, just drop the old partition. It is instant and keeps your indexes clean.

beats.title: Retention Strategy
beats.narration: Keep your events long enough to cover your Kafka retention and any potential manual replay window. Automate the cleanup, and your database will stay fast indefinitely.

beats.title: The Full Architecture
beats.narration: You now have a complete, reliable, and scalable event-driven pattern. Use the Outbox for atomic publishing and the Inbox for idempotent consumption. Your microservices are now truly resilient.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
